utterances.text: Okay. Good evening. I'm Christine o' Rourke and I'm the sustainability coordinator for the Marin Climate and Energy Partnership. Thanks for having me here tonight. I'm going to give you just a very brief overview of the 2023 greenhouse gas emissions inventory. This is for community wide emissions and 2023 is the latest year for which we have all the data that we need in order to, to produce these inventories. There's always a lag in the data of about a year, you know, about a year and a half before we have all the data that we need. So as I said, I'm with mcep Climate and Energy Partnership, and that is a partnership of all of the Marin jurisdictions plus some of our special districts. So tam, MCE and the Marin Water are members and we've been working together since 2007 to implement our, our climate action Plans. We also do these annual greenhouse gas emissions inventories. So we do the community wide every year and then we do local government inventories every five years or so. And as a reminder, these inventories that we do are called activity based inventories. And that's in comparison to what would be called a consumption based inventory. So we're only looking at a subset of, of all emissions from a household. We're looking at emissions from activities that occur within the San Rafael boundary. A consumption based inventory would include upstream emissions and things from life cycle emissions. So the chart here on the right is the emissions in 2023. And most of the emissions, two thirds are coming from the transportation sector. And of that about 80% come from passenger vehicles. The rest are mostly commercial vehicles, then a bit from public transit. The next largest slice of this pie is comes from the use of natural gas in the built environment. And then we have much smaller sectors. So built environment electricity is down to only 2% and waste is at 3%. Water and wastewater is 1% and off road is 1%. I've compared this to the 2022 emissions. So you can see kind of the change. Basically the electricity emissions went down. The emission factor actually is about half what it was in 2022. And that was because of the additional renewable and greenhouse gas free electricity that went into the power mix that both P and G and E&MCE provided in 2023. So that shrunk that piece of the pie from 6% to 2%. Natural gas actually went up from 26% of the pie to 27%. Natural gas in general went up 5% between 2022 and 2020, 2023. And it really is because it's due to a variability in the weather. So 2023 was most likely a colder year, colder winter than 2022. So natural gas, and most of this natural gas, a lot of it is being used to heat residents, residences. We saw similar increases across the board in the Marin jurisdictions. All went up about 4 or 5%. Except for the city of Nevado. Transportation emissions actually went down about 2%. But just because it's such a big slice of this pie and the other sectors shrank. So it's actually showing here that it went up 67%. So relatively it went up, but the actual number went down a little bit. And then overall, this is a look back to 2005. That's the year that we started doing inventories, or that we have all the data that we need in order to produce annual inventories. And then we estimate 1990 emissions per California Air Resources Board guidance, which is 15% below the 2005 level for 1990. So in the year 2023, emissions were down 24% below the 1990 level. And you can see that that's been steadily going down since peaking around 2007, 2008. The city's goal is the same as the state goal, which is to reduce emissions 40% below the 1990 level by the year 2030. So we have seven more years to attain that goal. And then. And you can see that in the dotted line. I don't know how clear that is on your, on your screen. And then the next dotted line below that is the long term state goal. So in 2045, the state is targeting zero net emissions. And 85% of that would come from mitigating or reducing emissions at the source. Then the other 15% would come from carbon dioxide removal strategies like sequestration, carbon capture, that sort of thing. So just a few sector highlights, and here I'm comparing the data from 2005 to 2023. So overall, electricity emissions are down 93% since 2000. And that's due to the lower carbon intensity of electricity. Again, the utility providers have been adding a lot of renewable and greenhouse gas free content into their power mixes. Electricity use overall is down 23%. I will note that that is purchased electricity. So that doesn't account for the electricity that is being generated from, like, rooftop solar. So the actual electricity would be higher than 2023% natural gas use and emissions, they're kind of go in lockstep. And that's down 10% overall since 2005. So even though it went up 5% between 2022 and 2023 overall down 10%, transfer transportation emissions are down 25%. I'm sorry, 24%. And so vehicle miles flat is essentially vehicle miles traveled or VMT is essentially flat. So since 2005. So all of those emissions reductions are coming from better fuel efficiency in the vehicles that are on our road as well as some zero emission vehicles. Zero emission vehicles are full battery, the electric vehicles as well as plug in hybrid electric vehicles. In 2023, just over 9% of the passenger vehicles on the road in Marin county are registered, I should say registered. Trent county residents were zero emission vehicles. It's a little bit lower in San Rafael. It just over 7% in San Rafael. And so the climate action plan target Is to have 25% zero emission vehicles traveling in San Rafael to be zero emission vehicles by the year 2030. So we're on our way and I have a slide to kind of demonstrate that coming up. And then waste emissions are down almost, almost by half. And that's due to the lower organic content in the landfill waste because that is where the emissions come from. And when the waste decomposes and the landfill and it creates methane, some of that escapes into the atmosphere. Overall waste disposal in landfills is down 20%. So at this point being 2025, we're beginning to get some questions about where are we headed and are we on the right track? Track. So I have a couple of slides to just throw some ideas out there. I don't have a crystal ball, don't know exactly what's going to happen. But the chart here on the left is the zero emission vehicle growth rate from 2010 to 2024. I've added the 2024 data in here and you can see that it's steadily climbing. And in fact it's got the last year it went up 21% and it's been at that rate kind of in the low 20 percentiles for the last few years. And so if we project out and this now if the chart on the right is projecting out, if we just grow the population of zero emission vehicles by 21% each year, by the year 2030 we would get to 41%. And again the cap target is 25%. Now of course, as a market matures, the growth rate slows down. But this is Just showing, you know, what the range of possibilities are. And then the other thing I wanted to share with you is this trend line. So the green line here is the actual emissions that I showed you before, just kind of depicted a little differently. And then the dotted orange line are the emissions reductions that are needed in order to meet the local San Rafael target. The dotted blue line, that fainter line, is the trend line. So that's the trend in emissions reductions between 2005 and 2023. And then if we just extend that trend line out the next few years, so if emissions continue to reduce at the same average reduction over the past, what would that be? 2005, 13, whatever years we would have emissions, the emissions would be lower than the target. So that is to say that the city is kind of on the right track. Now, of course, the earlier emissions have been a little easier to get. A lot of that happened from mce and that was essentially done. Although, I mean, the city had a big role in playing in creating mce, but that is something that kind of was done for people. So going forward it's, you know, a lot of the low hanging fruit I should say has been picked. So it may be a little bit more challenging to keep that growth rate up, but it is within the realm, I would say, of possibilities. My last slide, there are just a couple of corrections in the report that we wanted to get on the record here. It was on, on the. It's in the executive summary and it's talking about how many more emissions reductions are needed to meet the goal. And there was a typo. So the emissions that are needed is 64,755 metric tons to meet the 2030 target. And in order to meet the 2045 target, the emissions reductions are 245,995. And it had said 257,280. So it's. We're actually doing better than what was stated in the report. So. Okay, so I believe now we are going to stop and I'm happy to answer any questions. This is Corey, that you might have.

So tonight we adjourn our meeting in memory of Joan Thayer, a beloved San Rafael resident of of 47 years who devoted her life to public service. Joan was the second woman ever to serve on the San Rafael City Council and she truly paved the way for those of us who followed. It's remarkable to reflect that the first and third woman to serve on this council still live here in San Rafael. And tonight the 4th, the 5th and the 6th and 7th are sitting together on this dais. We really are standing on the shoulders of those who came before us, and Joan was one of those shoulders. I was fortunate to know Joan personally and to benefit from her wisdom, generosity and steady support over the years. She led with both heart and conviction, and she set a high standard for public service grounded in compassion and integrity. After two terms on the City Council, she went on to serve as Marin County's assessor recorder for 16 years, earning the respect of everyone she worked with. Her leadership and commitment to community continue to shape San Rafael today. We honor her legacy with deep gratitude and send our heartfelt condolences to her family. This meeting is now adjourned in honor of Joan Thayer.
